cap-reasoning-at-4k-per-response.name: cap-reasoning-at-4k-per-response
cap-reasoning-at-4k-per-response.title: Cap each response's reasoning at 4K tokens instead of 8K, so long single-response deliberation turn…
cap-reasoning-at-4k-per-response.hypothesis: Now a single response may think for up to 8,192 tokens before it has to act. The responses that use more than 4K are mostly not the agent's decisions. They are reconstructions of upstream tickets, commits and release notes, guesses about what tests will check, counting or identifier loops, and long mental execution of code that one command could run. Each costs minutes and stays in the context of every later request, because past reasoning is replayed. With the server stopping reasoning at 4,096 tokens, the model has to act with what it has: run the check, read the file, or make the edit. Its reasoning so far is still in context for the next response, so a real design chain carries on after one tool call instead of being lost. Fewer output tokens and minutes per task, with the same work done.
cap-reasoning-at-4k-per-response.evidence: In the parent's 26 runs, 13 responses had more than 4,096 reasoning tokens, in 9 runs (7 passed, 2 failed). They are django-10973 t13 4.1K (ticket and commit recall) and t17 8.2K (counting loop); django-12273 t9 6.2K (commit dates, which led to a `git log` date check), t11 5.2K (release-note recall), t16 7.1K and t27 8.2K (repeating, trimmed by the guard); django-13128 t15 5.0K; django-7530 t15 8.2K (repeating recall of later source); matplotlib-22871 t7 5.5K (upstream PR recall); sphinx-7985 t6 4.9K ("what the hidden tests might look like"); sympy-13974 t3 4.1K; sympy-14248 t21 8.2K (loop); and sympy-15976 t15 8.2K. About two thirds are recall, test-guessing or loops. The rest are real design reasoning (12273 t16, 13128 t15, 13974 t3). Above 4,096 these responses held 29.9K of the 404.6K output tokens (7.4%). The decisions that lost the diverged runs (10973, 9281, 15987) were made in short responses of 2.7K or less, so the cap neither causes nor fixes them. In a try run on an Easter-date formula bug, the cap stopped a response at exactly 4,096 tokens in the middle of mentally evaluating the formula for one year. The model then wrote a script to check every term instead. Over 480 s the cap fired 5 times in 14 requests, and every capped response still made a tool call. The parent on the same repo hit its 8K cap once in 17 requests. Neither changed a file within 480 s, so in that window the cap cost no progress.
cap-reasoning-at-4k-per-response.predicts: No response's reasoning goes over ~4.1K tokens. "reasoning hit the budget" shows up in about 25–35% of runs, against ~10% at 8K. Output tokens per task fall by 8–15% and minutes per task fall with them, mostly in the long tail (10K+ token runs). Requests per task rise by 0–1. The pass rate stays within noise of the parent. It's wrong if passes drop by 2 or more tasks per run, mainly on long design-heavy tasks where the cut lands mid-design. It's also wrong if output tokens per task don't fall by at least ~5%, which would mean the model just re-derives the cut reasoning in the next response.

cap-runaway-thinking.name: cap-runaway-thinking
cap-runaway-thinking.title: Cap each response's reasoning at 8K tokens, and don't let a cut or looping response end the run
cap-runaway-thinking.hypothesis: Now a single response can think for 20K–113K tokens. Almost always the model is trying to recall an upstream fix or a list of identifiers from memory, and that often turns into a loop of counting numbers. Such a response either burns many minutes, or ends with the intended tool call buried inside its reasoning (or cut at the output cap). Then there is no real tool call, so the run stops with whatever is on disk, sometimes nothing. With `thinkingBudgets.medium = 8192`, the server ends reasoning at 8K tokens and the model goes on to answer. An extension (`runaway-guard.ts`) covers the cases where that still goes wrong. If the last response ended reasoning-only, was cut at the length limit, wrote its tool call as text, or hit the budget and made no call, `agent_before_settle` adds one short message and asks for another turn (at most 2 in a row and 4 per run). A thinking or text block that was cut at the length limit, or that loops, is trimmed to its first 2,000 characters at `message_end` so it doesn't sit in every later request. In any repo, this bounds the cost of one bad response, and the run keeps working instead of ending empty.
cap-runaway-thinking.evidence: In the parent's 1,990 responses, 11 had more than 8,192 output tokens, nearly all of it thinking,, spread over 9 runs (3 passed, 6 failed): django-11477 (34K/53K/15K), 13033 (10K), 13089 (25K), 14404 (113K), 15037 (23K), matplotlib-22871 (23K), sphinx-7985 (17K), sympy-14248 (79K) and 15976 (50K). Every one of them was recall or a loop ("let me search my memory", "the instances include 11618, 11890, …"), not design work. Those 11 responses hold 444K of the batch's 1.49M output tokens, about 354K of it beyond the 8K cap; in the 3 passed runs they were the same kind of ramble and only cost time. Three runs ended on such a response with no real tool call, and all three failed: in matplotlib-22871 and sympy-14248 (both diverged tasks, passing in 2/3 and 1/3 runs) the counting loop ended in `</tool_call>` inside the reasoning, so the run stopped with no diff. django-14404 was cut at the output cap after 113K tokens. These are the only 2 no-diff runs and the only output-cap run in the batch. Responses of 4K–8K tokens include some real design work (16454 t2, 13974 t9/t18), so the cap isn't set lower. Tries: with a 100-token budget the model made a tool call after 4 of 5 forced cuts, and the guard handled the fifth. A live replay of a thinking-only looping response was trimmed, nudged once, and the run went on to edit, verify and finish. A normal run stayed quiet.
cap-runaway-thinking.predicts: No response's reasoning goes over ~8.2K tokens. Runs that end on a reasoning-only or length-cut response go from about 3 in 75 to about 0, and so do no-diff runs caused by them. "acted" should show "reasoning hit the budget" on roughly 10–15% of runs and a continuation on a few percent. Expect equal or slightly more passes (the empty endings on tasks that other runs pass) and clearly fewer output tokens and minutes in the heavy tail, about 15–25% of total output tokens. It's wrong if passes drop (cut reasoning hurting fixes), if output tokens don't fall because the runaway carries on into visible text (length endings with "trimmed" entries), or if most continuations come right after real final answers and change nothing.

cap-thinking-and-review-at-finish.name: cap-thinking-and-review-at-finish
cap-thinking-and-review-at-finish.title: Cap reasoning at 8K per response and keep accidental endings going, then review the diff against th…
cap-thinking-and-review-at-finish.hypothesis: The parent's runs go wrong at their ending in two separate ways. In one, a single response thinks for 20K–113K tokens (recall or a counting loop) and the run ends with no real tool call or is cut at the output cap, often leaving no diff. In the other, the agent ends as soon as it believes its fix is right, and the diff quietly misses something the issue states (literal expected output, the title's requirement) or was never tested after the last edit. This package puts the two changes that each moved their behavior together in one extension (`finish-guard.ts`) plus `thinkingBudgets.medium = 8192`. Reasoning stops at 8K. A response that ends the run by accident (cut, reasoning-only, a tool call written as text) gets a short nudge to go on (at most 2 in a row and 4 per run), and looping or cut blocks are trimmed from the context. The first time the agent really finishes, it sees the task next to its `git diff HEAD`, whether a test ran after its last edit, and gets one requirement-by-requirement check. They share one `agent_before_settle` handler, so they don't both fire on the same stop the way two stacked extensions would. The accidental-ending nudge goes first, and the review waits for a real finish. A capped response that does answer counts as a real finish, so the review replaces the redundant "capped" nudge there. The review also keeps the task text from the first message, so it still works after a compaction has dropped that message (the ported version silently skipped the review then). Bounding one bad response and checking the final diff against the stated task both help in any repo, and they go after different failures, so their gains should add up.
cap-thinking-and-review-at-finish.evidence: Diverged tasks show both failure modes. sympy-14248 failed: a 79K-token counting loop ended with `</tool_call>` inside the reasoning, so there was no diff. matplotlib-22871 (23K) and django-14404 (113K, cut at the cap) went the same way. In the parent's 1,990 responses, 11 went over 8K, across 9 runs (6 failed). django-13089 passed but spent 25K tokens recalling an upstream ticket. On the finishing side, sphinx-9281 failed after printing `= ValueA` against the issue's literal `MyEnum.ValueA` and calling it a match. django-12774 failed after deleting the uniqueness check "matching upstream ticket #29574" with no test run after the edit. django-13012 raised the right concern and then dismissed it on recall. In the tree, cap-runaway-thinking scored +1.5 ± 2.1 (kicked in on 30/153 runs; output tokens 20.5k→18.6k, no-patch runs 1→0). review-diff-against-task-at-finish scored +1.2 ± 1.9 (146/153 runs; +13% tokens, about +3 requests). Its review turns in "broken" runs (django-15987, matplotlib-22871) left the diff unchanged, so the review itself didn't cause those losses. Both variants' fixed and broken lists are mostly the parent's noisy diverged tasks. Replays: a fake-event replay of the 14248 sequence trimmed the loop, nudged once, reviewed once at the real finish and ended. A capped answer before the review got the review and no nudge, a git failure or a compacted context still produced a review, and an aborted run was left alone. Live try on a small repo with an Enum/Flag expected-output issue: the review fired once, the agent reran the issue's example and the tests, and the run ended. A scratch copy with a 150-token budget showed `settings.json` cutting reasoning at 150 tokens and "reasoning hit the budget" being logged.
cap-thinking-and-review-at-finish.predicts: "finish review" appears on nearly every run. "reasoning hit the budget" appears on about 15–20% of runs, "continued after …" on a few percent, and never together with a review on the same stop. No response's reasoning goes over about 8.2K tokens. Runs with no patch or ending at the output cap go to about 0. Output tokens per task land near the parent's (cap −9%, review +13%) with about 3 more requests. Passes should rise by about the two gains together (+2 to +3 of 51), more than either part alone. It's wrong if passes don't beat both parent and the better single variant, if long reasoning responses still appear, or if tokens rise well above the review variant alone.

complete-test-results-review-only-untest.name: complete-test-results-review-only-untest
complete-test-results-review-only-untest.title: Test runs come back with their full verdict, and the finish review runs only when the change is unt…
complete-test-results-review-only-untest.hypothesis: The agent pipes almost every test run through a filter (`| tail -3`, `| grep -E "^(Ran|OK|FAILED)"`). The filter often cuts the verdict or the failing tests' names, and guessed test labels that name no module look like ordinary errors, so the agent reruns the same suite just to read what it already ran. When it stops, the parent always adds a finish review. After a change whose tests passed, that review hardly ever changes the diff: it re-runs the example and the tests at the run's largest context, or turns into guessing what upstream did. This package merges two variants. test-feedback.ts (from test-runs-recover-cut-verdict-and-bad-la) puts the cut verdict and failing test ids back into the same result and names labels that match no test module. The gate from finish-review-only-on-untested-change keeps the review only for an objective gap: no change, no test since the last edit, or new untracked files. Merging them adds two points. (1) A test run counts only if it ran something: "No module named pytest", "Ran 0 tests", "no tests ran", "collected 0 items", file-not-found, or only label `_FailedTest` errors leave the change untested, and the review names that empty run. (2) Each run is judged by its result as the model saw it, test-feedback's recovered verdict included. If the last real test run after the last edit reported failures (label errors don't count), the review stays and asks the agent to settle each failure by the system prompt's rule on existing tests. That is the one situation where the parent's review changed a diff for a reason. A passing tested change ends at once. A failing or untested one still gets its second look.
complete-test-results-review-only-untest.evidence: Read start to finish: django-15987 both runs, sphinx-9281 failed, django-14672, sympy-12096, astropy-8872 and matplotlib-25332 passed, astropy-13977, sphinx-7985 and sympy-13974 failed. Only 3 of the parent's 26 runs edited after their first stop. django-10973 (passed) was untested and keeps the review. django-15987 (failed) had dismissed an existing test its change broke, and the review reverted that part; its last test run reported `FAIL:`, so the review stays. sphinx-7985 only moved a CHANGES bullet. In the passed runs the review re-ran the example and tests and changed nothing. django-7530 spent 3+ turns at 35% context re-proving a fix it had already tested. I replayed the gate over the parent's transcripts with this package's patterns. It skips the review in 16 of 26 runs. It keeps it in 3 untested runs (django-10973, django-14608, sympy-14248) and in 7 whose last test run failed: django-15987, plus six with failures that were there before the change (astropy-8872, django-16454, matplotlib-22871, scikit-learn-14710, sympy-12096, sympy-15976). In the 16 skipped runs, 29 of 475 turns (6.1%) came after the first stop, all at peak context. The empty-run check matched 22 test commands in 15 runs (15 `python -m pytest` with no pytest, 5 bad `runtests.py` labels, 2 others) and changes no gate decision on these runs. It decides the gate in a run like test-runs-recover-cut-verdict-and-bad-la's broken django-15987, whose only test after the edit was a bad label. Test feedback kicked in on 50 of 51 and 51 of 51 runs. On the grandparent it cut requests 37→34 and output tokens 21.9k→18.3k (+2.0 passes). Its port to this parent did not repeat that (35→37 requests, -1.5 passes). Both are within noise.
complete-test-results-review-only-untest.predicts: "skipped finish review: change tested and passing after last edit" on about 55-70% of runs. "finish review (failing tests)" on about 20-30% and "finish review (untested change...)" on about 10-15%. "added the test results a filter cut" on most runs and "explained missing test labels" on about 15-35%. Requests per task should fall by about 1-3 (about 1.1 skipped review turns per run on average, plus rerun-only test turns), and input tokens by more than output tokens, since the skipped turns are the largest. Passes stay within noise of the parent, and a dismissed self-caused failure still gets reviewed. It's wrong if passes drop by 2 or more per run, or if the skip share is high but requests and tokens per task don't fall against the parent.

edit-lists-tests-for-changed-code.name: edit-lists-tests-for-changed-code
edit-lists-tests-for-changed-code.title: edit/write results list the existing tests that reference the function or class just changed
edit-lists-tests-for-changed-code.hypothesis: Right now `edit` returns only "Successfully replaced N block(s)". The agent then decides on its own whether to test and where, and it often guesses: it runs a nearby module, invents a test path or label, or runs nothing. With this change, after a successful `edit`/`write` of a tracked, non-test Python file, the tool reads `git diff HEAD` for that file and finds the innermost function(s) and class around each changed spot. It then appends the existing test files, and the test functions in them, that reference those names, found with `git grep -w` over `tests/` dirs and `test_*.py`-style files. At most 2 names and 4 files are listed per edit, each name once per run. Dunder and generic names are skipped, as are names referenced from more than 15 test files. When nothing is found, nothing is added. So the agent learns, at no cost in turns, where the behavior it just changed is pinned down, and runs those tests before finishing. A fix that breaks current behavior the issue never asked to change then fails an existing test while the agent can still react. That is a common way real fixes go wrong in any repo.
edit-lists-tests-for-changed-code.evidence: In 73 of 75 parent runs the agent edited a non-test .py file, so the change can kick in on nearly every run. The two runs where it can't are runaway runs with no diff. 10 runs ran no tests after their last edit; 5 of them failed (django-10973, django-12774, django-14404, matplotlib-22871, sympy-14248). In the diverged django-12774 pair, the failing run deleted the uniqueness check in `in_bulk` and never ran tests/lookup, whose `test_in_bulk_non_unique_field` pins that check. The passing run did run tests/lookup. django-10973 searched tests/backends and never found tests/dbshell. On cost, 16 bash errors came from guessed paths that don't exist, and several runs spent turns working out test labels (django-13012, django-13128, django-12774). In a replay of the in_bulk moment on a small repo, the edit result listed `test_bulk_lookup_non_unique_field` and its siblings. The agent ran that test file and, in its final message, named the listed constraint test. When one listed test already failed before the change, the agent checked it with `git stash`, set it aside, and finished without chasing it.
edit-lists-tests-for-changed-code.predicts: The "acted" entry appears on most runs (more than 70%). The share of runs that run a listed test file after their last edit goes up, and runs that never test after editing go down. There are fewer errors from guessing test paths or labels. Passes should be equal or higher, mostly on tasks where a plausible fix breaks a neighbouring existing test. Tokens should stay about flat: tool output grows by about 100-300 tokens per run, and a few search turns go away. The idea is wrong if the listed files are run no more often than in the parent, or if runs get longer (chasing failures in listed tests the agent didn't cause) with no gain in passes.

explain-missing-test-labels.name: explain-missing-test-labels
explain-missing-test-labels.title: Explain test labels that name no module, right in the bash result
explain-missing-test-labels.hypothesis: The agent often guesses dotted test labels for label-taking runners (a `runtests.py` over a directory of test packages, `python -m unittest`) that don't exist: `contenttypes` for `contenttypes_tests`, `lookups` for `lookup`, `auth`, `save`, `queries.BulkUpdateTests`, `db_functions.datetimes`. The runner reports each one as an ordinary-looking error (`ERROR: x (unittest.loader._FailedTest)`, counted in `FAILED (errors=1)`). The agent's own `| tail` / `| grep "^(Ran|OK|FAILED)"` filter usually hides which test errored. So it reruns the suite to dig out the traceback, does `git stash` baseline checks, runs `python -c "import contenttypes"`, and sometimes concludes its fix broke something. Or it believes tests ran that never did. With this change, a `tool_result` hook (bash only) parses the command: `cd` tracking, quotes, redirections and runner options. It checks every label against the files under the runner's test root. Only when a label names no package, module or class does it append a short note saying which labels don't exist, that the error is from the label and not the code, that those tests did not run, and which labels are close (with the test modules inside the closest package, or where a named class actually lives). It never blocks or rewrites a call, and stays silent when every label resolves. One look at the note replaces the rerun-and-diagnose loop, so the agent runs the tests it meant to run.
explain-missing-test-labels.evidence: In the parent's runs, `_FailedTest` / "Failed to import test module" shows up in 25 of the 45 runs on a `runtests.py`-style repo (19 passed, 6 failed), 66 times in all, almost always from a made-up label. Those are only the ones a filter didn't hide. The worst cases are long failed runs. django-15957 spent about 13 requests (turns 84–97, context over 60%) chasing `contenttypes`, even checking whether the test suite had deleted directories. django-14792 spent about 9 requests (turns 55–65) on `timezone`, `forms_tests.model_fields`, `template_tests.test_tz` and `template_tests.tz`, including a `git stash` baseline. django-11477 (t61–70) chased `admin`, `urlpatterns_init`, `syndication` and `urls_reverse` with stash checks. Passed runs pay too: django-12273 (t27–39 on `save`, plus `python -c "import save"`), django-13012 (17 hits: `values`, `querysets`, `subqueries`), django-13128, django-17084 and django-13028. Replayed live with try-variant on a small repo with a label-style runner. The note fired on both wrong labels (`text_utils`, `slugify`) with the right package and its test modules. When the agent then guessed a class name that doesn't exist, the next note listed the module's real classes, and the agent's next run used a valid label. The note stayed silent on valid labels. In a third replay, after the repair, the note fired on the issue's own wrong label. The agent read it ("the actual module is `text_utils_tests.tests`") and spent no requests chasing the error. In offline checks on commands taken from the transcripts it flags the bad labels above with the right suggestion (contenttypes_tests, lookup, auth_tests, save_delete_hooks, db_functions.datetime, queries.test_bulk_update.BulkUpdateTests). It stays quiet for valid labels, `$var` labels, heredocs, plain greps that mention runtests.py, non-label runners, file-path labels (`test_x.py`), classes re-exported through `import *`, and unittest packages installed outside the repo.
explain-missing-test-labels.predicts: "acted" ("explained missing test labels") should show on roughly 30–40% of runs (about half of the runs on runtests.py-style repos, rarely elsewhere). On those runs, fewer requests should go to re-running a suite only to see what errored, to `import <label>` probes and to `git stash` baseline checks after a label error. Expect about 1–3 fewer requests on a typical affected run and many more on the long ones, with total tokens down mostly through fewer late, high-context requests. Passes should hold, maybe rise slightly where a misread `errors=1` sent the agent after its own fix, or where the intended tests never ran. It's wrong if acted runs keep the same number of runtests reruns and diagnosis commands as the parent's (the note is ignored), if tokens per acted run don't fall, or if passes drop (for example, if the agent starts dismissing real errors as label problems).

failing-tests-rerun-without-change.name: failing-tests-rerun-without-change
failing-tests-rerun-without-change.title: Failing test runs after an edit get an automatic baseline: the harness reruns the same command with…
failing-tests-rerun-without-change.hypothesis: When a test run after its edit fails, the agent has to work out whether the failures are its own. It does that by hand: `git stash`, rerun, `git stash pop` (the parent's prompt tells it to), then compares two long outputs by eye or with ad-hoc grep/diff. Sometimes it forgets to pop. Now a `tool_result` hook steps in when a single-call bash test command fails after an edit. It reruns that exact command once with the tracked changes stashed (60-300 s timeout, pytest cache off), restores them, and checks that the diff is byte-identical. Then it appends one short note: the summary line without the change, plus which failing test ids appear only with the change, which fail without it too, and which fail only without it. Results are cached per HEAD+command, at most 6 runs. It never runs for commands that touch git state, write files or use `--lf`/`--ff`, for parallel calls, or after 40 min. Exact attribution in the same turn saves the round trips. It also stops the agent from chasing failures that were already there, and from waving off regressions it caused as "pre-existing".
failing-tests-rerun-without-change.evidence: Manual stash baselines show up in 13 of 26 parent runs (37 `git stash` commands), in passed and failed runs alike. Examples: sympy-14248 (11 stash commands over turns 41-80, diffing failure lists by hand), matplotlib-25332 (6 stash commands, the stash left unpopped at turn 36), django-7530 (ran the full suite twice to compare), astropy-8872, django-16454, sympy-12096, and the failed astropy-13977 and sphinx-7985. Replaying the trigger rules over the parent transcripts, it would have fired in 20 of 26 runs (18 passed, 2 failed: django-15987 and sphinx-7985), on about 49 distinct failing commands. In a try-variant run with the real model, it fired on the agent's first pytest run, which had a failure that existed before the change. The agent got "Failing without your change too, so not caused by it: tests/test_locale.py::test_utf8_locale" and moved on with no stash of its own. In mock replays the tree and stash came back intact in these cases: staged and new files, a baseline that writes into tracked files, a baseline that hangs past its timeout, an untracked file that blocks the pop, and a directory that isn't a git repo (skipped).
failing-tests-rerun-without-change.predicts: `acted` entries "reran failing tests without the change" or "showed the cached baseline for failing tests" on roughly 60-75% of runs. "baseline could not restore the change" should be about 0. The agent's own `git stash` commands drop sharply (from about 1.4 per run to under 0.5). Runs where it fires use 1-3 fewer requests, and tokens fall a little. Wall time goes up by one extra test run per distinct failing command: replayed on the parent's runs, that is about 10 s per run where it fires and 47 s at most. Passes hold or rise slightly. Signs it's wrong: manual stash baselines persist at similar rates; requests and tokens don't fall on runs where it fired; passes drop, for example final diffs that leave tests listed as "Failing only with your change" still failing.

finish-review-only-on-untested-change.name: finish-review-only-on-untested-change
finish-review-only-on-untested-change.title: Run the finish review only when the change is empty, untested since the last edit, or leaves new un…
finish-review-only-on-untested-change.hypothesis: Now every run that stops gets one more round: the harness shows the task and the diff and asks for a requirement-by-requirement re-check. When the agent has already run a test command after its last edit, that round almost never changes the diff. It re-runs what was just run, or turns into a long guess at what upstream did or what unseen checks expect, all at the run's largest context. With this change the review fires only on an objective gap: no change at all, no test command since the last edit, or untracked files the agent created (files already untracked before its first tool call don't count). A tested, non-empty change ends the run when the agent stops. The diff handed in is the one it had before the review, so passes should hold, with fewer requests, tokens and minutes per run. The runaway guard, thinking cap, system prompt and the review text itself are unchanged.
finish-review-only-on-untested-change.evidence: In the parent's 26 runs only 3 edited anything after the first stop. django-10973 (passed) added a `runshell_db` alias after about 3.4K tokens of guessing hidden-test names; this variant keeps the review there because the edit was untested. django-15987 (failed) restored an error message and narrowed the fix to one expression, and still failed. sphinx-7985 (failed) only moved a CHANGES bullet. fresh-eyes-finish-review reports zero review edits in the grandparent's runs. The review phase is where hidden-test/upstream talk peaked: 63, 22, 13 and 6 such sentences in django-10973, sphinx-9281, django-15987 and sphinx-7985 (3 of these 4 failed), and about 0 in most passed runs. In sphinx-9281 (failed) the review turn is where the agent wrote "The hidden tests probably verify the upstream fix", tried `pip download`, and kept `ValueA` anyway. I replayed each run's tool calls through the extension's own test and edit patterns. 23 of 26 runs had a non-empty change tested after the last edit at the first stop, so the review would be skipped. The other 3 (django-10973, django-14608, sympy-14248) keep it. In those 23 runs the review cost 45 of 773 requests (5.8%) and 20.2K of 405K output tokens (5.0%), all at peak context. No run left throwaway files in the repo. try-variant on toy repos: a fix tested with pytest ended at the agent's first stop with the skip entry. An unchecked fix got "finish review (untested change)" and one more round. A mocked-API check of the settle hook covers no git, git failing, a capped stop, a context over the limit, pre-existing untracked files, a leftover repro script, `git stash pop` after a test, and an empty diff; every run ends after at most one review.
finish-review-only-on-untested-change.predicts: "skipped finish review: change tested after last edit" on about 80-90% of runs, and "finish review (...)" on about 10-20%. Requests per task fall by about 1.7 (about 6%) and output tokens by about 5%. Input tokens fall by more, about 10%, since the skipped turns re-send the largest context of the run, and minutes fall a little. Passes stay within noise of the parent, because the skipped rounds almost never changed the diff. It's wrong if passes drop by 2 or more per run, or if the skip share is high but requests and tokens per task don't fall.

finish-review-probes-same-cause-inputs.name: finish-review-probes-same-cause-inputs
finish-review-probes-same-cause-inputs.title: Finish review makes the agent probe other inputs that hit the same cause, and extend a fix that onl…
finish-review-probes-same-cause-inputs.hypothesis: Today the agent fixes the exact trigger in the issue's example, re-runs that example, sees it pass and calls the fix "minimal" and done. The parent's once-per-run finish review (requirements, example, tests) only re-checks that same example, so a fix that misses a second way into the same bug goes out unchanged. With this variant, when there is a change, the finish review gets one more step. The agent names the cause its change removes (the code that went wrong, not the symptom). It then picks 2-4 other inputs that reach the same code by another route and tries them in one short script. It looks first at other uses of the same value in the changed function or class, then at the same state reached another way (it greps the repo for other code that sets the same attribute or calls the same function), then at another type or form of the value, and at every function or option the task names. It extends the fix only where the problem the task reports still shows. It is told to stay on the task's code path: leave other backends, printers, formats and subclasses alone, add no unasked behavior, use inputs that are easy to build, run the script once, and leave other problems alone. In general coding this is the difference between "the reported example works" and "the bug is fixed". The step comes at the one moment the agent has the change, the repro and a working environment in hand.
finish-review-probes-same-cause-inputs.evidence: In the parent, the runs that failed with a working fix for the example usually had too narrow a fix, not a wrong one. django-15987 (diverged): in its finish review the failing run narrowed its fix to the `len(set(...))` duplicate check and explicitly decided not to normalize the value in the second check (`app_dir in fixture_dirs`) of the same function ("Minimal fix it is"). fresh-eyes-finish-review.name: fresh-eyes-finish-review
fresh-eyes-finish-review.title: Run the finish review in a fresh context, without the agent's earlier reasoning
fresh-eyes-finish-review.hypothesis: The parent's finish review runs in the same context that produced the change, so the agent re-reads its own rationale and confirms it ("matches upstream", "those tests encode the old bug, they'll be replaced") instead of checking the change. From the review message onward, this variant sends each request with only the system prompt, the task, and the review message plus what follows it. The earlier history is left out of the requests, not deleted from the session. The review message carries everything an outside reviewer needs: the `git diff HEAD` (stat + patch, up to 16K chars), untracked files, the test commands the agent ran, the tail of the last test output (and whether it ran after the last edit), and a checklist. The checklist steps are: map every requirement to a hunk; undo hunks no requirement needs; run the task's example and copy expected vs actual output word for word; run the existing tests for the touched code and fix the change, not the test, unless the test asserts the reported bug; change nothing without a concrete reason. Without the author's reasoning in view, the reviewer judges the change by the task and the repository, the way a code reviewer does. That catches scope creep into neighbouring code paths and regressions the author had already argued away, which happens on any codebase. The runaway-thinking guard, the 8192-token thinking cap and the nudges are the parent's, unchanged. With no git, or no change at all, there is no diff for an outsider to judge. The review then keeps the parent's in-context form, with the parent's 100K-token skip.
fresh-eyes-finish-review.evidence: In all 26 of the parent's runs, plus the 8 runs where it fixed or broke a task against its own parent, the in-context review led to zero edits. It's a confirmation ritual, so the parent's gain came from the thinking cap, not the review. Its 3 failures each passed through that review with the flaw in view. In sympy-15976 the agent also changed the content printer, which the issue never mentions, and broke `test_content_symbol`. The review dismissed the failure as "old tests encoding the bug". The passing baseline run left that printer alone, and 5 of the 7 variants' failed runs of this task made the same extra change. In sympy-14248 a 201-line diff touched core arithmetic helpers and broke 11 tests, all dismissed, while passing runs changed only the printers (45-49 lines). In sphinx-9281 the review noticed that its output differed from the expected `MyEnum.ValueA` and dismissed it as matching a recalled upstream fix. I replayed this with the model against mock repos, using a multi-turn tool loop, at the review moment. A change that also edited an unrequested renderer and broke its test was reverted to the minimal diff in 3 of 3 samples. A correct fix whose only failing test pinned the reported bug was kept in 3 of 3 samples, so no false undo. A single-shot fresh replay of the sphinx moment still misread or recalled in 2 of 3 samples, which is why step 3 now asks for verbatim side-by-side output. End to end with try-variant on a synthetic repo, two runs ended cleanly with the correct diff, and the review request fell from ~4.3K to ~2.9K prompt tokens. A no-change run kept the in-context review, and a mock-API test covered no git, compaction, aborted runs and the "review changed the diff" record.
fresh-eyes-finish-review.predicts: "fresh-context finish review" fires on almost every run. "review changed the diff" rises from 0 (the parent) to a few-to-10% of runs, mostly reverting unrequested hunks or fixing a literal expected-output mismatch. Tasks failed through scope creep or dismissed regressions (like sympy-15976 and sympy-14248) pass more often, and passes rise by 1-3 out of 51. Review-phase requests are a fraction of the parent's (system + task + review instead of the whole history), so input tokens on long runs fall. The reviewer adds about 2-6 calls to re-run the example and tests, so output rises slightly. It's wrong if "review changed the diff" stays near 0. It's also wrong if runs that passed in the parent start failing after a review change, i.e. the reviewer undoes needed parts or breaks a working fix for lack of context.

issue-evidence-system-prompt.name: issue-evidence-system-prompt
issue-evidence-system-prompt.title: Replace pi's generic system prompt with one that settles expected output, failing tests, sibling co…

Match the issue's literal expected output exactly when it shows one. For each new test failure, quote the issue sentence that calls wrong what the assertion checks (through the issue's code or a caller, not a sibling), or rework the change until the test passes. Leave a sibling implementation alone if changing it breaks its own tests. Run the callers' tests when a shared helper changes. Treat a remembered upstream fix as a guess. The rules are in view from the first request, so they shape the decision when it's made, not after the agent has committed to it. Diffs for issues that name one code path should touch fewer sibling implementations, and results should match an issue's literal expected output more often. review-diff-against-task-at-finish.name: review-diff-against-task-at-finish
review-diff-against-task-at-finish.title: Review the diff against the restated task once, before the run may end
review-diff-against-task-at-finish.hypothesis: The agent ends a run as soon as it believes its fix is right. By then the issue text is dozens of tool calls back, and in the failed runs the final diff quietly misses something the issue states (the title's requirement, the exact expected output) or was never tested after the last edit. One extra request where everything already holds, 2-5 where it runs the example or tests or fixes something; tokens up roughly 10-15% on passed runs. run-tests-tool.name: run-tests-tool
run-tests-tool.title: Add a run_tests tool: compact pass/fail report, runner discovery, and a before/after comparison tha…
run-tests-tool.hypothesis: Now the agent runs tests through bash and spends turns on the plumbing rather than the fix. It pipes the run through `tail -N` and loses the summary (Django prints "Destroying test database…" after it), then reruns with `grep -E "^(OK|FAILED|Ran)"`, then again with `grep -A30 "^ERROR:"` to see what failed. And it checks whether a failure is pre-existing with `git stash` / rerun / `git stash pop`, which risks a tree left without its changes. A `run_tests` tool takes the plain test command, keeps the whole output in a log, and returns the summary line, each failing test with its error line, the labels that could not be loaded, and the last lines. When the command can't start a runner, it lists the runners the repo has. With `compare_with_original` it runs the same command on a copy of the repo at HEAD (ignored build files kept, imports pointed at the copy) and reports which failures are new with the change, which were already failing and which the change fixed. Fewer turns go to test plumbing, regressions the change causes are named instead of being written off as "pre-existing", and the working tree is never stashed.

In try-variant runs on small repos the model used `run_tests` unprompted, followed the runner hint after `python` was missing, and used `compare_with_original` to set aside two pre-existing failures in one call.
run-tests-tool.predicts: Most runs that test call `run_tests` ("acted" on roughly 60–80% of runs, with "run_tests with comparison" on 15–30%). Bash calls that run test commands drop by more than half, and plumbing reruns (the same suite rerun only to see its summary or traceback, `git stash` baseline checks) mostly disappear. Runs that test should need about 2–5 fewer requests each, with similar or slightly fewer output tokens and as many passes or slightly more. It's wrong if the agent ignores the tool ("acted" on under 20% of runs), if requests and tokens don't fall in the runs that use it, or if passes drop.

test-feedback-with-same-cause-review.name: test-feedback-with-same-cause-review

Replays: I drove the real hooks with a stub `pi` and ran the rewritten commands in bash on a Django-style runner that prints its verdict and then 16 teardown lines. - `tail -3` came back with "Ran 7 tests / FAILED (failures=1) / FAIL: test_at_tier (…)". - A grep that kept only the verdict got the failing id and not the verdict a second time. - A bad class label got the label note and the cut verdict. - When the verdict was visible, nothing was added. The same held for pytest's visible "no tests ran" and for a visible wrapped sympy summary. - `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` still held the runner's status. Live `try-variant` runs: - After the fixes, `python3 tests/runtests.py 2>&1 | tail -5` showed only teardown lines. The note added "Ran 806 tests … OK", and the agent's next message was "All 806 tests passed", with no rerun. - In an earlier run, `python3 -m tests.runtests | tail -30` went untapped under the old pattern, and the agent reran it with a grep. That run is what led to the second fix. - The note stayed silent when `tail -15` already showed "Ran 6 tests / OK", and when pytest's "no tests ran" was visible. - All 6 runs finished normally with the parent's finish review and an empty pi.err.
test-runs-recover-cut-verdict-and-bad-la.predicts: "added the test results a filter cut" should show on about 60–90% of runs, and "explained missing test labels" on about 15–35%, mostly on runtests.py-style repos. Test runs that come right after a filtered run, with no edit in between, should drop well below the parent's 38 in 26 runs. That's about 1–3 fewer requests on runs that test, and more on long Django and sympy runs. Output tokens and minutes should fall by roughly 10–15%, and passes should hold at the parent's level. It's wrong if requests and tokens per run don't fall against the parent, if those reruns stay as common, if the agent spends new turns reading the saved logs, or if passes drop, for example because a real error gets waved off as a label problem.

test-runs-show-cut-results-and-bad-label.name: test-runs-show-cut-results-and-bad-label
test-runs-show-cut-results-and-bad-label.title: Bash test runs get back the verdict and failing tests a filter cut, and bad test labels explained,…
test-runs-show-cut-results-and-bad-label.hypothesis: The agent runs tests through bash and almost always pipes them through a filter (`| tail -5`, `| grep -E "^(Ran|OK|FAILED)"`). The filter often cuts the verdict (Django's runner prints "Destroying test database…" lines after it), or shows `FAILED (errors=2)` without saying which tests failed. And when the agent guesses a dotted label that names no module (`models`, `values`, `auth`), the runner reports it as an ordinary-looking error. Then the agent reruns the suite only to see what it already ran, probes with `import <label>` or `git stash`, or takes empty output for "all pass". This package adds one bash `tool_result` hook to the parent that merges two variants. A `tee` before the first filter keeps the unfiltered output, and when the filter hid the verdict or failing test ids, the result gets them back (test-summary-survives-output-filters). Every label of a label-taking runner is checked against the files on disk, and a missing one is named along with the closest real labels (explain-missing-test-labels, unchanged). The two overlap on the `_FailedTest` errors that missing labels cause. Those are explained once, as label problems, and left out of the "failing" list. A failing test now counts as already shown only when its whole id is visible, so a real import error is never hidden behind a label note. With the outcome of the run it just made in front of it, the agent skips rerun-only turns and stops reading a label error or an empty filter as a result.
test-runs-show-cut-results-and-bad-label.evidence: I replayed the parent's 26 transcripts through the merged code. The tap fires on test runs in 24 runs (67 calls). In 21 runs, 38 of those results showed no verdict at all, and 17 of those were followed directly by another test run (12 runs). In 5 runs, 10 results showed `FAILED (…)` without naming the failing tests. `_FailedTest` label errors appear in 7 of the 14 Django runs. Moments: in django-13012 at t14→t15, the agent got `FAILED (errors=2)` and reran the suite with `grep -B2 -A20 "^ERROR"` only to see the errors. They came from its labels `values` and `group_by`. Then at t16→t17, `tail -3` cut the verdict ("tail -3 cut off the results"), and it reran again. django-12273 passed but took 91 requests and 17 min. At t50, `tail -20` showed only "Destroying test database" lines. At t51–52, `models` gave "Ran 1 test … FAILED (errors=1)" and was rerun with `head`. At t60 and t84 more guessed labels (`auth`, `admin`, `db_migrations`) cost a turn each. In sympy-14248 (failed, 141 requests) at t70–71, `python -m unittest … | grep -i "fail\|error"` printed nothing and the agent concluded "test_str all pass!", but no tests had run. I replayed it live with try-variant on a small repo with a Django-style runner. The `tee` went in every time and the note stayed silent when the verdict was visible (2 runs). When `tail -5` showed only teardown lines, the note added "Ran 0 tests … OK", and the agent's next message said "0 tests were run in that label" (run 3). In offline replays, `lookups`, `text_utils` and `…BulkUpdateTest` were explained with the right labels, label errors weren't listed twice, and a real failure and a real import error in the same run were still listed. On its own, explain-missing-test-labels kicked in on 17/51 runs (it predicted 30–40%) for +0.5 tasks per run, not proven. test-summary-survives-output-filters has not been run.
test-runs-show-cut-results-and-bad-label.predicts: "added the test results a filter cut" on most runs (60–90%), and "explained missing test labels" on about 15–35%, mostly on runtests.py-style repos. Test runs that only repeat the previous one with a new filter, tail length or `grep ERROR`, and `import <label>` probes after a label error, should drop well below the parent's rate (17 reruns after a result with no verdict, in 26 runs). That's about 1–3 fewer requests on runs that test, and more on long Django runs. Fewer late, high-context requests mean fewer input and output tokens. Passes should hold or rise slightly, where a run would otherwise misread a hidden or empty result. It's wrong if requests and tokens per run don't fall against the parent, if reruns right after a tapped run stay as common, if the agent spends new turns reading the saved logs, or if passes drop (for example, if real errors get waved off as label problems).

test-summary-survives-output-filters.name: test-summary-survives-output-filters
test-summary-survives-output-filters.title: Bash test runs piped through a filter keep their summary and failing test names
test-summary-survives-output-filters.hypothesis: The agent almost always pipes test runs through a filter (`runtests.py … 2>&1 | tail -5`, `| grep -E "^(OK|FAILED|Ran)"`). The filter often cuts the runner's verdict or the names of the failing tests: Django's runner prints "Destroying test database…" lines after the summary, and `FAILED (errors=4)` says nothing about which tests failed. So the agent reruns the same suite with a different filter just to see what it already ran. This variant changes the bash tool for these commands only. It inserts a `tee` before the first filter to keep the runner's unfiltered output in /tmp. When the filtered result is missing the verdict or the failing test ids, it adds them to the result (unittest/Django, pytest, sympy and a few other formats), along with the saved file's path. If the filter left no output at all, it adds the output's last lines instead. Anything else the agent sees is unchanged. Telling the agent the result of the run it just made should remove a rerun-only turn, and the waiting time that goes with it, whenever a filter hides the outcome. It needs no new tool for the model to adopt. That matters because run-tests-tool's separate tool was used but barely cut requests.
test-summary-survives-output-filters.evidence: In the parent's 26 runs, 193 test-runner commands were piped through a filter. 62 of those results showed no verdict at all (ANSI stripped). 41 were followed directly by another test run, in 16 runs: sympy-14248 had 12, django-7530 had 5, and django-13128, django-14404 and sphinx-8593 had 3 each. django-7530 turns 35→36 show it: "The output got cut off at the tail end before displaying the OK/FAILED lines" leads to the same command again with `| grep`. cap-runaway-thinking's broken django-12273 does the same thing: "only the line about destroying the DB is displayed — I need the summary line. Let me re-run it". Another 50 or so results showed `FAILED (errors=N)` without naming the failing tests, e.g. django-12273 "Ran 302 tests … FAILED (errors=4)" and django-10973. Replaying the parent's commands through the rewriter: it would tap 166 calls and add a note to about 100 of them, in 22 of 26 runs (20 passed, 2 failed). In try-variant on a small repo with a Django-style runner, `python3 tests/runtests.py 2>&1 | tail -5` got back the cut "Ran 188 tests / FAILED (failures=1) / FAIL: test_…" lines. The agent then went straight to that test instead of rerunning the suite. Heredocs, loops, background jobs, `| head`, unbalanced quotes and a missing `tee` leave the command untouched.
test-summary-survives-output-filters.predicts: Fewer test→test pairs where the second run only changes the filter or the tail length, fewer `git stash`-free reruns just to read a verdict, about 1–2 fewer requests in runs that run tests, and a few percent fewer output tokens. Pass rate should stay the same. It should rise slightly at most, where a run that rarely saw which tests it broke now sees them. The "acted" entry "added the test results a filter cut" should appear in most runs. The idea is wrong if the share of filtered test runs followed directly by another test run doesn't drop well below the parent's 41/193. It is also wrong if requests and output tokens per run don't fall, or if the agent spends new turns reading the saved logs.

trace-tool-shows-executed-code-path.name: trace-tool-shows-executed-code-path
trace-tool-shows-executed-code-path.title: Add a `trace` tool that runs a Python example and returns the call tree of repository functions it…
trace-tool-shows-executed-code-path.hypothesis: Before editing, the agent finds where behavior comes from by grep and reading, and traces the code paths in its head: the parent's runs make a median of 7 grep/read/sed calls before the first edit, and only 8 of 26 runs run the issue's example before editing. When the wrong value is built in a layer below the first grep match, or comes through a second path, the agent fixes the layer it found, or spends many turns tracing paths by hand. The new `trace` tool runs a snippet under a profiler and returns its output plus a compact call tree of the checkout's functions that ran: who called whom, call counts, and the simple return values (str, number, bool, small containers; other objects show only their type name, so no project code runs during the trace). Long trees are cut by depth, and a `focus` regex shows the paths into one function. One line in the tool rules says when to use it: a runnable example gives a wrong value without a traceback, before the first edit. It says to skip it when a traceback already names the line, when there is nothing runnable, and for tests. So the agent picks the function to change from what actually ran, in one call instead of a chain of greps. That helps on any Python repository.
trace-tool-shows-executed-code-path.evidence: In sphinx-9281, the failed run fixed the signature formatter and got `ValueA`, which differs from the issue's literal `MyEnum.ValueA`. The passed run fixed the value-description function (`object_description`) that produced the text. A trace of the issue's example lists both functions with their return values. In django-12273, both runs spent about 30 requests reading and mentally tracing `save()` paths before the first edit (20 explore calls). The failed run missed the `pk = None` route. Long pre-edit exploration also shows in sympy-14248 (17 explore calls), sympy-15976 (13), django-13128 (15), sphinx-9281 (12) and sphinx-8593 (11), in both passed and failed runs. Tool tests: without the rule line, the model ignored `trace` on two small replays and localized by grep. With the rule line, on a copy of a 3.6K-line package with a bug two calls below the public API, it called `trace` in one of two runs, as its second action. That tree showed `_is_not_suffix x5 -> True` (also for `'post3'`) under `_compare_compatible`, the exact cause, and the run fixed that function. That run also used `trace` to check its edit and got about 10K chars per call, so after the first edit the default tree is now 40 lines: a replay got 8 depth-limited lines with `[+N nested]` marks. On an in-process pytest session (12.8K calls), the tracer took 0.3 s and returned a 108-line tree. Syntax errors, exceptions, `sys.exit`, `unittest.main()`, pickling, timeouts (the partial tree is kept) and "no repository code ran" all return a readable result.
trace-tool-shows-executed-code-path.predicts: "acted" entries ("trace tool run before|after the first edit") appear in at least 30% of runs, mostly before the first edit. Those runs make fewer grep/read calls before the first edit than the parent's median of 7. Fewer fixes land in a caller or sibling of the function that produces the wrong value, so passes are the same or better, with output tokens per task the same or lower. Uptake in testing was 1 of 2 runs, so this rests on the rule line being followed. The idea is wrong if uptake stays under 15% of runs, or if runs that use `trace` take more requests or tokens with no gain in passes.

work-from-repo-not-recall.name: work-from-repo-not-recall
work-from-repo-not-recall.title: Steer the agent off reconstructing upstream fixes from memory, back to the repo's code
work-from-repo-not-recall.hypothesis: The agent treats most tasks as a known issue in a public project and spends its longest reasoning trying to recall "the actual upstream fix": ticket and PR numbers, commits, a later version's code. It can't check any of it, and much of it is invented. That's where runs go wrong. Either the recall rambles into a 20K–80K-token loop that ends with no tool call, or a made-up "upstream" becomes the yardstick and outweighs the issue text and the agent's own concerns. With this change, `APPEND_SYSTEM.md` tells it to work from the repo: a recollection is a guess to check, and the issue's stated behavior plus the existing tests are what the fix is judged against. `recall-guard.ts` enforces this where the behavior shows up. After a response whose reasoning tries to reconstruct an upstream fix, it appends a short note to that response's first tool result (at most 3 per run, at least 5 responses apart). If the response that would end the run leans on such a recollection, the agent gets one more turn to check the change against the task (once per run). That turn says "make the edit now" if no file was changed. Working from the code in front of you instead of an unverifiable memory is how coding goes in any repo. It should cut wasted reasoning and remove one source of confidently wrong fixes.
work-from-repo-not-recall.evidence: The shipped detector matches in 67 of the parent's 75 runs (48 of 56 passed, all 19 failed), first at response 3 (median). Matching responses are about 21% of all responses but hold 62% of output tokens in passed runs and 75% in failed ones. Diverged tasks, failing side: in django-12774 the agent deleted the uniqueness check "matching the upstream fix for ticket #29574" (an invented ticket) and never ran the existing tests. In django-13012 the last turn raised the right concern, then dismissed it as "matches the upstream Django fix (ticket #31050) exactly". In sphinx-9281 the agent wrote a `stringify` from a recalled "PR #10010" that prints `ValueA` where the issue expects `MyEnum.ValueA`, and kept it "consistent with upstream". In sympy-14248 one 79K-token response ("Have to rely on my memory of upstream fixes") ended with no diff, and matplotlib-22871 also ended with an empty patch while chasing "the upstream fix". The passing sides worked from the code. Passed runs waste tokens on it too: django-15037 spent most of its 56K output tokens recalling "#33309". The final response leans on recall in 5 of 19 failed runs (django-12774, django-14404, matplotlib-22871, sphinx-9281, sympy-14248) and in 2 of 56 passed runs (django-13033, psf__requests-6028). Replay on a `packaging` checkout with a planted bug: both the parent ("The actual upstream fix (packaging PR #520)") and this variant ("The upstream fix (around packaging PR #664)") recalled by their third response, so the prompt alone doesn't stop the habit. The note then fired on that tool result, no further recall followed, and the fix was correct.
work-from-repo-not-recall.predicts: "recall nudge" should fire on most runs (about 80–90%) and "recall check at finish" on about 5–10%. Recall phrases per run and the thinking share should drop. Output tokens per task should fall clearly, mostly in the long tail: fewer 10K+ responses, fewer reasoning-only endings and fewer runs with no diff. Passes should hold or rise, mainly on tasks whose failing runs were a recall-driven fix or a recall loop. It's wrong if responses matching recall per run don't fall against the parent (the model ignores both the prompt and the note), if output tokens don't fall, or if passes drop (recall was helping more than it hurt).
